doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Starting trumpet after discovering his father's swing records
summary: Kellso got interested in trumpet at about ten through his parents' Swing Era records, then found his father had played; Harry James was his first idol.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe. We’re filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. I’m pleased to have Jon-Erik Kellso, trumpeter and jazz musician with us today. So let’s be honest, what’s a nice young man like you doing playing jazz music?

Oh, well, I got interested when I was really young. My parents were both into the Swing Era music, you know they grew up during that time and they had a lot of good old records around the house, so when I was about ten years old I got interested in playing the trumpet, and then after I decided to play trumpet I found out that my father was a trumpet player and had played in some swing bands during the World War II days. And I found some of his old records around, and got interested in it.
Did you pick the trumpet then without him kind of pushing you into it?

Exactly. I didn’t even know that he had played trumpet. So I had a built-in first trumpet teacher there. He hadn’t played in years but it was kind of amazing — he was able to pick up his old horn, which he still had, and play pretty well, considering how many years it had been since he had touched it. He kind of sounded a little bit like Harry James. So that was my first trumpet idol.
Not a bad guy to sound like.
Yeah. That was his big idol, and that was my first trumpet idol because those were the records that he had.
Well it’s perhaps fortunate he didn’t try to push you into it, because as kids, you might have rebelled or something. And it’s a nice coincidence you picked it on your own.
Yeah, right. It worked out quite well.
